description:
We're five Systems Engineering students from the University of Lima, Peru. We love exploring how AI, data, software, cybersecurity, automation and electronics can solve real problems.

Inspired by Project Hail Mary, we're here to learn, try bold ideas and build something we're proud of. We may not have all the answers, but we know how to work together and keep asking questions.

Six-Seven minds. One mission. A little controlled chaos. Amaze, Amaze, Amaze! 🪨

details:
What it does and how it works

UPRIGHT is an offline health copilot for a four-person crew on long-duration missions. It answers one question no dashboard does: what body will you land with? Spaceflight damage is slow, silent and cumulative: bone loss, blood pooling in the neck veins, eye changes, radiation, latent viruses waking up. No single day feels different, and Earth can be 20 minutes away.

Future Self: each astronaut sees their body today next to their projected body on landing day, as 3D anatomy with a time slider. Landing Readiness answers “can I stand, see, move and think when gravity returns?” Every countermeasure (exercise, water, sleep) bends that trajectory.

Measure → Understand → Act → Verify → Escalate:

Measure: a two-minute daily check (glove-sized keypad, rejects impossible values) and continuous watch data with activity context.

Understand: a deterministic rules engine compares each value with safe ranges and with the person’s own baseline. Compound rules then cross indicators, because NASA’s five hazards make each other worse.

Act and verify: UPRIGHT gives one action, re-checks after a set time and verifies the result.

Escalate: if the problem is not solved, it writes a one-screen brief for the flight surgeon, with the arrival time and the earliest possible reply given the communication delay.

A real “Why?”: every status opens a plain-language explanation: what it means, your case (your value, your usual, what changed), what to do now and when we check again. It can be read aloud.

Crew of four: each astronaut has their own profile, baselines and alerts. A medical-officer view shows everyone at once, lets a crewmate respond for someone who is incapacitated, and runs crew-level rules (several headaches at once → check the cabin air; a fever → protect the others; a solar storm → everyone to the shelter).

Mission simulator for judges: pick an astronaut, a destination (ISS, Moon, Mars transit or surface) and one of five hazard scenarios (neck-vein clot risk, kidney stone, solar storm with virus reactivation, CO₂ build-up with vision changes, sleep loss with slow reactions). Then watch UPRIGHT detect, explain, act and escalate.

Landing debrief and phases: explains what the body will face on Mars (0.38 g), the Moon (0.16 g) or Earth, and what changes during launch, spacewalks and entry.

Benefits

Astronauts who are not physicians can spot silent problems early, understand them and act in under three minutes a day, without waiting for Earth. The crew medical officer sees the whole crew, and the flight surgeon receives a short, prioritised brief instead of raw data.

Intended impact

The goal is earlier detection of conditions that would otherwise go unnoticed until landing, and more Earth-independent medical operations for Moon and Mars missions. On Earth, the same offline, explain-then-act design could serve remote and high-altitude communities in Peru, where a doctor is also hours away.

Tools and technologies

Code: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand and IndexedDB.

3D anatomy: Three.js with Z-Anatomy/BodyParts3D models (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Hardware: Web Bluetooth for real heart-rate bands (tested with consumer bands).

Delivery: an installable offline web app (PWA), and an Electron Windows app that blocks every network request.

Optional on-device AI: WebLLM with Qwen2.5-1.5B, used only to reword explanations.

Quality and hosting: Vitest (168 automated tests), GitHub Actions and Vercel.

Design: pen.dev.

Creativity

A trajectory, not a status: instead of a dashboard of today’s numbers, astronauts see their future self, with every action changing it.

Rules that compound: they follow how NASA’s hazards interact, for one person and across the whole crew.

Explanations, not citations: the “Why?” explains in plain words instead of listing references.

A simulator for judges: it lets anyone see the whole loop in three clicks.

Factors we considered

Safety: a deterministic, tested rules engine decides every status. AI never does; the local AI only rewords, and a safety check discards its output if it adds numbers, diagnoses, drugs or links.

Honesty: every threshold is labelled as an official NASA figure or as a prototype value. Stale or missing data is never shown as OK.

Real mission constraints: no internet, communication delays, under three minutes a day, use with gloves, sex-specific physiology and a four-person crew.

Usability: status is never colour alone (icon + word + colour), the app is fully bilingual (English/Spanish), and it has a night mode.

Limits: it is not a medical device. The app names no drugs or doses, and all crew data in the demo is fictional or simulated.
